claim: SARS-CoV-2 is estimated to have infected some 10% of the world's population.
source: SARS-CoV-2, the viral causative agent of COVID-19, is estimated to have infected some 10% of the world's population, killing a confirmed ~ 5 million but likely considerably more.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the estimated infection rate of SARS-CoV-2 presented in the introduction.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 has killed a confirmed ~5 million people but likely considerably more.
source: SARS-CoV-2, the viral causative agent of COVID-19, is estimated to have infected some 10% of the world's population, killing a confirmed ~ 5 million but likely considerably more.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the death toll from COVID-19 presented in the introduction.

claim: Inequities in vaccine distribution challenge current and future containment of the pandemic.
source: Despite the great promise of vaccines, the pandemic is ongoing; inequities in vaccine distribution, waning immunity, the biological and behavioral diversity of the human population, the emergence of viral variants that compromise monoclonal therapies and vaccine efficacy, all challenge current and future containment (Diamond et al., 2021; Lavine et al., 2021; Fraser et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2021a; Wang et al., 2021b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature discussing challenges to pandemic containment.

claim: Waning immunity challenges current and future containment of the pandemic.
source: Despite the great promise of vaccines, the pandemic is ongoing; inequities in vaccine distribution, waning immunity, the biological and behavioral diversity of the human population, the emergence of viral variants that compromise monoclonal therapies and vaccine efficacy, all challenge current and future containment (Diamond et al., 2021; Lavine et al., 2021; Fraser et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2021a; Wang et al., 2021b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature discussing challenges to pandemic containment.

claim: The emergence of viral variants that compromise monoclonal therapies and vaccine efficacy challenges current and future containment of the pandemic.
source: Despite the great promise of vaccines, the pandemic is ongoing; inequities in vaccine distribution, waning immunity, the biological and behavioral diversity of the human population, the emergence of viral variants that compromise monoclonal therapies and vaccine efficacy, all challenge current and future containment (Diamond et al., 2021; Lavine et al., 2021; Fraser et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2021a; Wang et al., 2021b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature discussing challenges to pandemic containment.

claim: Spike is the major surface envelope glycoprotein of the SARS-CoV-2 virion.
source: Spike (S), the major surface envelope glycoprotein of the SARS-CoV-2 virion, is key for infection as it attaches the virion to its cognate host surface receptor, angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) protein, and triggers fusion between the host and viral membranes, leading to viral entry into the cytoplasm (Zhou et al., 2020; Wrapp et al., 2020b; Walls et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature describing the spike protein.

claim: Spike attaches the virion to angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) protein.
source: Spike (S), the major surface envelope glycoprotein of the SARS-CoV-2 virion, is key for infection as it attaches the virion to its cognate host surface receptor, angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) protein, and triggers fusion between the host and viral membranes, leading to viral entry into the cytoplasm (Zhou et al., 2020; Wrapp et al., 2020b; Walls et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature describing the spike protein's function.

claim: Spike triggers fusion between the host and viral membranes, leading to viral entry into the cytoplasm.
source: Spike (S), the major surface envelope glycoprotein of the SARS-CoV-2 virion, is key for infection as it attaches the virion to its cognate host surface receptor, angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) protein, and triggers fusion between the host and viral membranes, leading to viral entry into the cytoplasm (Zhou et al., 2020; Wrapp et al., 2020b; Walls et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature describing the spike protein's function.

claim: The spike protein monomer is ~140 kDa, or ~180–200 kDa including its extensive glycosylation.
source: The spike protein monomer is ~140 kDa, or ~180–200 kDa including its extensive glycosylation, and exists as a homotrimer on the viral surface.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the molecular weight of the spike protein.

claim: The spike protein exists as a homotrimer on the viral surface.
source: The spike protein monomer is ~140 kDa, or ~180–200 kDa including its extensive glycosylation, and exists as a homotrimer on the viral surface.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the oligomeric state of the spike protein.

claim: Spike is composed of two domains: S1, which contains the host receptor binding domain (RBD); and S2, which undergoes large conformational changes that enable fusion of the viral membrane with that of its host.
source: Spike is highly dynamic and is composed of two domains: S1, which contains the host receptor binding domain (RBD); and S2, which undergoes large conformational changes that enable fusion of the viral membrane with that of its host (Li et al., 2003; Li, 2016; Letko et al., 2020; Watanabe et al., 2020; Hsieh et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature describing the structure and function of the spike protein.

claim: The major target of immunotherapeutics has been the RBD.
source: Based on its requirement for entry, the major target of immunotherapeutics has been the RBD (Hartenian et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2020; Baum et al., 2020; Finkelstein et al., 2021; Korber et al., 2020; Trigueiro-Louro et al., 2020; Barnes et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on immunotherapeutics targeting the RBD.

claim: Emerging variants, particularly RBD point mutants, have evolved to bypass the most potent neutralizing human antibodies.
source: Major immunotherapeutic strategies to date have focused on immune sera and human monoclonal antibodies; however, these therapies now face the emergence of variants, particularly RBD point mutants, which have evolved to bypass the most potent neutralizing human antibodies (Wang et al., 2021b; Liu et al., 2021a; Weisblum et al., 2020; Garcia-Beltran et al., 2021; Starr et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on viral variants and antibody escape.

claim: Nanobodies are the smallest single-domain antigen binding proteins identified to date.
source: Nanobodies are the smallest single-domain antigen binding proteins identified to date, possessing several potential advantages over conventional monoclonal antibodies.
evidence: This is a factual statement about nanobodies.

claim: Nanobodies are derived from the variable domain (VHH) of variant heavy chain-only IgGs (HCAb) found in camelids.
source: Nanobodies are derived from the variable domain (VHH) of variant heavy chain-only IgGs (HCAb) found in camelids (e.g., llamas, alpacas, and camels).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the origin of nanobodies.

claim: Nanobodies can bind with very high affinities comparable to the very best antibodies.
source: They can bind in modes different from typical antibodies, covering more chemical space and binding with very high affinities (comparable to the very best antibodies) (Jovčevska and Muyldermans, 2020; Muyldermans, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on nanobody properties.

claim: The small size of nanobodies (~15 kDa) allows them to bind tightly to otherwise inaccessible epitopes.
source: Their small size (~15 kDa) allows them to bind tightly to otherwise inaccessible epitopes that may be obscured by the glycoprotein coat, as well as minimizing issues of steric hindrance of multiple antibodies binding to adjacent epitopes as observed with larger immunoglobulin G molecules (Corti et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature on nanobody properties.

claim: Nanobodies are highly soluble, very stable, lack glycans, and are readily cloned and produced in bacteria or yeast.
source: Nanobodies are also highly soluble, very stable, lack glycans, and are readily cloned and produced in bacteria or yeast (Muyldermans, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature on nanobody properties.

claim: Nanobodies have low immunogenicity.
source: They have low immunogenicity (Revets et al., 2005; Jovčevska and Muyldermans, 2020; Bannas et al., 2017) and can be readily 'humanized' (including Fc addition), modified to alter clearance rates, derivatized, combined for synergistic activity, and multimerized to improve characteristics (Chanier and Chames, 2019; Vincke et al., 2009; Duggan, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on nanobody properties.

claim: Nanobodies can be delivered by nebulization deep into the lungs.
source: Beyond typical administration methods, a major advantage of nanobodies is their potential for direct delivery by nebulization deep into the lungs (Wölfel et al., 2020; Nambulli et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on nanobody delivery methods.

claim: There are 453 nanobodies available against SARS-CoV-2 spike.
source: To date, there are 453 nanobodies available against SARS-CoV-2 spike and those that are available primarily recognize regions of RBD with many subject to escape variation (Niu et al., 2021; Raybould et al., 2021; Schoof et al., 2020; Xiang et al., 2020; Koenig et al., 2021; Huo et al., 2020a; Pymm et al., 2021; Hanke et al., 2020; Custódio et al., 2020; Esparza et al., 2020; Wrapp, 2020a; Dong et al., 2020; Ye et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on available nanobodies.

claim: Available nanobodies primarily recognize regions of RBD with many subject to escape variation.
source: To date, there are 453 nanobodies available against SARS-CoV-2 spike and those that are available primarily recognize regions of RBD with many subject to escape variation (Niu et al., 2021; Raybould et al., 2021; Schoof et al., 2020; Xiang et al., 2020; Koenig et al., 2021; Huo et al., 2020a; Pymm et al., 2021; Hanke et al., 2020; Custódio et al., 2020; Esparza et al., 2020; Wrapp, 2020a; Dong et al., 2020; Ye et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on available nanobodies.

claim: The authors generated a large repertoire of nanobodies that exploit the available epitope and vulnerability landscape of SARS-CoV-2 spike protein.
source: To address the urgent need for strongly neutralizing and escape resistant nanobodies, we generated a large repertoire of nanobodies that exploit the available epitope and vulnerability landscape of SARS-CoV-2 spike protein.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's objective and approach.

claim: The resulting repertoire provides a plethora of synergistically potent and escape resistant therapeutics.
source: The resulting repertoire provides a plethora of synergistically potent and escape resistant therapeutics.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's findings.

claim: The authors optimized each step of their nanobody generation pipeline to yield hundreds of high-quality, highly diverse nanobody candidates.
source: Thus, we built on our existing nanobody generation pipeline (Fridy et al., 2014a), further optimizing each step, explicitly designing it to yield hundreds of high-quality, highly diverse nanobody candidates (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's methodology, supported by a reference to Figure 1A.

claim: The authors took advantage of the straightforward procedure of llama immunization and the powerful natural affinity maturation processes in vivo.
source: In this way, we took advantage both of the straightforward procedure of llama immunization and the powerful natural affinity maturation processes in vivo (Thompson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's methodology, supported by a citation.

claim: The authors affinity-purified VHH domains from the immunized animals' sera against spike S1, S2, or RBD domains.
source: To identify VHH domains that bind spike, we affinity-purified VHH domains from the immunized animals' sera against spike S1, S2, or RBD domains using independent domains in this purification step to maximize epitope accessibility.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's methodology.

claim: Lymphocyte RNA was taken from bone marrow aspirates and used to amplify VHH domain sequences by PCR, which were sequenced to generate an in silico library representative of all VHH sequences expressed in the individual animal.
source: In parallel, lymphocyte RNA was taken from bone marrow aspirates and used to amplify VHH domain sequences by PCR, which were sequenced to generate an in silico library representative of all VHH sequences expressed in the individual animal.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's methodology.

claim: The affinity-purified VHH fragments were proteolyzed and the resulting peptides analyzed by LC-MS/MS.
source: The affinity-purified VHH fragments were proteolyzed and the resulting peptides analyzed by LC-MS/MS.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's methodology.

claim: The LC-MS/MS data were searched against the VHH sequence library to identify and rank candidate nanobody sequences using the Llama-Magic software package.
source: These data were searched against the VHH sequence library to identify and rank candidate nanobody sequences using our Llama-Magic software package (Fridy et al., 2014a; Fridy et al., 2014b) with a series of key improvements (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's methodology, supported by citations.

claim: The authors clustered CDR sequences to maximize sequence diversity and thus the paratope space being explored.
source: To maximize sequence diversity and thus the paratope space being explored, we clustered CDR sequences, revealing that many of the candidates form clusters likely to have similar antigen binding behavior.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's methodology.

claim: Partitioning of the clusters was performed by requiring that CDR3s in distinct clusters differ by a distance of more than three Damerau–Levenshtein edit operations.
source: Here, partitioning of the clusters was performed by requiring that CDR3s in distinct clusters differ by a distance of more than three Damerau–Levenshtein edit operations (Bard, 2007) – that is, each operation being defined by insertion, deletion, or substitution of an amino acid residue, or transposition of two adjacent amino acid residues (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's methodology, supported by a citation and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Virtually no overlap was observed between nanobodies directed against S1 versus S2 (4 out of 183 clusters show overlap).
source: This partitioning was found to be effective, in that virtually no overlap was observed between those directed against S1 versus S2 (4 out of 183 clusters show overlap).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on the clustering analysis.

claim: The lengths of the CDR3 candidates varied considerably, ranging from 3 to 22 amino acids in length.
source: The lengths of these CDR3 candidates also varied considerably, ranging from 3 to 22 amino acids in length.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on the sequence analysis.

claim: The use of two animals further expanded the paratope diversity in that only 4 out of 22 possible clusters from the second animal were observed to be shared with the first animal.
source: The use of two animals further expanded the paratope diversity in that only 4 out of 22 possible clusters from the second animal were observed to be shared with the first animal.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on the clustering analysis.

claim: Only 1 out of 109 S1-specific clusters (Damerau–Levenshtein ≤3) were shared by Xiang et al., 2020 and the present work.
source: In addition, we detected relatively little overlap between our CDR3 clusters and those observed by other groups; for example, only 1 out of 109 S1-specific clusters (Damerau–Levenshtein ≤3) were shared by Xiang et al., 2020 and the present work, indicating that our repertoires sampled extended regions of the available paratope space (see also below).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on comparison with published data, supported by a citation.

claim: 180 high-confidence candidates were selected for expression and screening.
source: Of the several hundred positives, 180 high-confidence candidates were selected for expression and screening.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's methodology.

claim: Of the 180 candidates, 66 were from S1 affinity purification, 63 from S2, and 51 from RBD.
source: Of these, 66 were from S1 affinity purification, 63 from S2, and 51 from RBD, numbered S1-n, S2-n, and S1-RBD-n, respectively.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's methodology.

claim: 138 candidates were validated by the binding screen: 52 against S1, 42 against S2, and 44 against RBD.
source: 138 candidates were validated by this screen: 52 against S1, 42 against S2, and 44 against RBD (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on the binding screen, supported by reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Only nanobodies in lysates with binding intensity >20% of the observed maximum across all those screened were chosen for follow-up study.
source: To eliminate candidates with weaker expression and binding affinity, only nanobodies in lysates with binding intensity >20% of the observed maximum across all those screened were chosen for follow-up study.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's methodology.

claim: This filtering identified the top 116 nanobodies that were purified for further characterization.
source: This filtering identified the top 116 nanobodies that were purified for further characterization (Tables 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's methodology, supported by reference to Tables 1 and 2.

claim: The group of 116 nanobodies retained a high sequence and paratope diversity.
source: While a few of these 116 nanobodies were chosen to share similar paratopes, overall, the group retained a high sequence and paratope diversity (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on sequence analysis, supported by reference to Figure 1C.

claim: All 116 nanobodies bound with high affinity, with >60% binding with KDs < 1 nM.
source: All bound with high affinity, with >60% binding with KDs < 1 nM, and two with single-digit picomolar affinities (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on SPR analysis, supported by reference to Figure 2.

claim: Two nanobodies bound with single-digit picomolar affinities.
source: All bound with high affinity, with >60% binding with KDs < 1 nM, and two with single-digit picomolar affinities (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on SPR analysis, supported by reference to Figure 2.

claim: 71 S1-binding nanobodies bind RBD.
source: While most S1-binding nanobodies bind RBD (71 nanobodies), 19 targeted non-RBD regions of S1 and 26 bind S2 (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on binding assays, supported by reference to Figure 2.

claim: 19 S1-binding nanobodies targeted non-RBD regions of S1.
source: While most S1-binding nanobodies bind RBD (71 nanobodies), 19 targeted non-RBD regions of S1 and 26 bind S2 (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on binding assays, supported by reference to Figure 2.

claim: 26 nanobodies bind S2.
source: While most S1-binding nanobodies bind RBD (71 nanobodies), 19 targeted non-RBD regions of S1 and 26 bind S2 (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on binding assays, supported by reference to Figure 2.

claim: The lower number of non-RBD S1 and S2 nanobodies likely reflects the highly antigenic nature of the RBD and the occlusion of non-RBD S1 regions and S2 due to the glycan shield of SARS-CoV-2 spike.
source: The lower number of non-RBD S1 and S2 nanobodies likely reflects the highly antigenic nature of the RBD and the occlusion of non-RBD S1 regions and S2 due to the glycan shield of SARS-CoV-2 spike (Grant et al., 2020; Watanabe et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings, supported by citations to published literature on spike glycosylation.

claim: There was no obvious bias in nanobody affinities for different domains of spike.
source: At the same time, we observed no obvious bias in nanobody affinities for these different domains.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on SPR analysis.

claim: Many nanobodies have fast association rates (kon ≥ 10+6).
source: While both high on rates and low off rates contributed to these high affinities, kinetic analyses underscore the generally fast association rates (many with kon ≥ 10+6) of these nanobodies (likely due to their small size and proportionally large paratope surface area), with many surpassing the kon of high-performing monoclonal antibodies (kon ~ 10+5) (Tian et al., 2020; Figure 2), a property that would benefit translation of these nanobodies into rapid therapeutics and diagnostics (Carter, 2006).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on SPR analysis, supported by citations and reference to Figure 2.

claim: Many nanobodies surpass the kon of high-performing monoclonal antibodies (kon ~ 10+5).
source: While both high on rates and low off rates contributed to these high affinities, kinetic analyses underscore the generally fast association rates (many with kon ≥ 10+6) of these nanobodies (likely due to their small size and proportionally large paratope surface area), with many surpassing the kon of high-performing monoclonal antibodies (kon ~ 10+5) (Tian et al., 2020; Figure 2), a property that would benefit translation of these nanobodies into rapid therapeutics and diagnostics (Carter, 2006).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on SPR analysis, supported by citations and reference to Figure 2.

claim: For nanobodies with apparently homologous paratopes, there was no correlation in their kinetic properties.
source: For those nanobodies with apparently homologous paratopes (Figure 1C), we found no correlation in their kinetic properties (Tables 1 and 2), demonstrating that even small paratope changes can strongly alter behaviors (Fridy et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on SPR analysis, supported by a citation and references to Figure 1C and Tables 1 and 2.

claim: RBD mutants represent a significant class of escape variants.
source: RBD mutants represent a significant class of escape variants (Garcia-Beltran et al., 2021; Greaney et al., 2021), leading us to employ two strategies to ensure the generation of numerous nanobodies whose binding (and virus-neutralizing activities) are resistant to emerging variants.
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to published literature on escape variants.

claim: The authors isolated a large diversity of high-quality anti-RBD nanobodies to maximize the probability of identifying ones that are refractory to escape.
source: First, we isolated a large diversity of high-quality anti-RBD nanobodies to maximize the probability of identifying ones that are refractory to escape.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's strategy.

claim: The authors deliberately targeted non-RBD regions of spike to reveal additional nanobody-neutralizing potential.
source: Second, to reveal additional nanobody-neutralizing potential, we deliberately targeted non-RBD regions of spike (see below) (Elshabrawy et al., 2012; Greaney et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's strategy, supported by citations.

claim: Six out of seven tested RBD-binding nanobodies retained their very strong binding to both B.1.1.7/20I/501Y.V1/alpha and B.1.351/20H/501Y.V2/beta variants.
source: Of the seven nanobodies tested, six of these (S1-1, S1-6, S1-RBD-9, S1-RBD-11, S1-RBD-15, and S1-RBD-35) retained their very strong binding to both variants, with only a modest reduction in affinity for S1-RBD-11 binding to variant B.1.351/20H/501Y.V2/beta (20–161 pM).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on SPR analysis.

claim: S1-23 binding to variant B.1.1.7/20I/501Y.V1/alpha was reduced from a KD of 17 pM to 230 pM.
source: For the seventh nanobody, S1-23, binding to variant B.1.1.7/20I/501Y.V1/alpha was only reduced from a KD of 17 pM to a still-respectable 230 pM, although its binding to variant B.1.351/20H/501Y.V2/beta was abolished (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on SPR analysis, supported by reference to Figure 2.

claim: S1-23 binding to variant B.1.351/20H/501Y.V2/beta was abolished.
source: For the seventh nanobody, S1-23, binding to variant B.1.1.7/20I/501Y.V1/alpha was only reduced from a KD of 17 pM to a still-respectable 230 pM, although its binding to variant B.1.351/20H/501Y.V2/beta was abolished (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on SPR analysis, supported by reference to Figure 2.

claim: It is the off rates that are most affected by these variants.
source: As expected (VanCott et al., 1994; Magnus, 2013; Steckbeck et al., 2005), it is the off rates that are most affected by these variants.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on SPR analysis, supported by citations.

claim: A high percentage of the nanobody collection is expected to remain resistant to escape mutants, including the B.1.617.2/21A/delta variant.
source: Nevertheless, based on epitope mapping (below) and our identification of nanobodies that recognize epitopes not altered in the emerging variant strains, we expect that a high percentage of our nanobodies will remain resistant to these escape mutants; this would now include the B.1.617.2/21A/delta variant (Campbell et al., 2021), making our collection a powerful resource for potential prophylactics and therapeutics.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the study's findings, supported by a citation.

claim: All but two nanobodies fall within a Tm range between 50 and 80°C.
source: These studies revealed a thermal stability range between 50 and 80°C, similar to published results of other properly folded nanobodies and indicative of their generally high stability (Muyldermans, 2013).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on DSF experiments, supported by a citation.

claim: The bulk of the nanobodies have a Tm ≥ 60°C.
source: These studies revealed a thermal stability range between 50 and 80°C, similar to published results of other properly folded nanobodies and indicative of their generally high stability (Muyldermans, 2013).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on DSF experiments, supported by a citation.

claim: Nanobodies remain fully active upon reconstitution after lyophilization, particularly in buffers lacking cryoprotectants.
source: In contrast to many conventional antibodies, nanobodies are also reported to remain fully active upon reconstitution after lyophilization, particularly in buffers lacking cryoprotectants (Schoof et al., 2020; Xiang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to published literature on nanobody properties.

claim: Freeze-drying without cryoprotectants revealed no significant effect on stability, kinetics, and affinity of a representative sample of nanobodies.
source: A representative sample from our repertoire was thus freeze-dried without cryoprotectants, reconstituted, then analyzed via SPR and DSF to determine whether their properties were compromised due to lyophilization. The results revealed no significant effect on stability, kinetics, and affinity (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on SPR and DSF experiments, supported by reference to Figure 2E and F.

claim: The nanobodies are able to withstand various temperatures and storage conditions without affecting their stability and binding.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that our nanobodies, like those published in other contexts (Xiang et al., 2020; Schoof et al., 2020), are able to withstand various temperatures and storage conditions without affecting their stability and binding.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the study's findings, supported by citations.

claim: 56 anti-RBD nanobodies were screened in pairwise combinations using biolayer interferometry.
source: 56 anti-RBD nanobodies were screened in pairwise combinations.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's methodology.

claim: Eleven representative anti-RBD nanobodies were used as a foundation to bin the remaining RBD nanobodies in the collection.
source: Eleven representative anti-RBD nanobodies were used as a foundation, selecting two or more representative nanobodies from each group to bin the remaining RBD nanobodies in our collection.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's methodology.

claim: The epitope binning approach revealed three large, mostly non-overlapping bins for RBD-binding nanobodies.
source: This approach revealed three large, mostly non-overlapping bins.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on epitope binning analysis.

claim: Each bin contained smaller, better-correlated clusters of nanobodies, indicating the presence of numerous distinct sub-epitope bins.
source: However, each bin contained smaller, better-correlated clusters of nanobodies, reflected by the dendrogram, indicating the presence of numerous distinct sub-epitope bins present within each larger bin, that is, discrete epitopes that partially overlap with other discrete epitopes in the same bin.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on epitope binning analysis.

claim: The gap statistic estimated at least eight epitope bins for RBD-binding nanobodies.
source: We calculated the gap statistic (Tibshirani et al., 2001), to estimate the optimal cluster number, discerning at least eight epitope bins (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on statistical analysis, supported by a citation and reference to Figure 3A.

claim: 16 non-RBD S1-binding nanobodies were binned in pairwise competition assays.
source: Using SPR, we binned 16 non-RBD S1-binding nanobodies and 19 S2-binding nanobodies in pairwise competition assays (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's methodology, supported by reference to Figure 3B and C.

claim: 19 S2-binding nanobodies were binned in pairwise competition assays.
source: Using SPR, we binned 16 non-RBD S1-binding nanobodies and 19 S2-binding nanobodies in pairwise competition assays (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's methodology, supported by reference to Figure 3B and C.

claim: Hierarchical clustering revealed as many as four S1-non-RBD bins and five S2 bins.
source: Pearson's correlation coefficients were used to hierarchically cluster these nanobodies, revealing as many as four S1-non-RBD bins and five S2 bins.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on epitope binning analysis.

claim: Mass photometry demonstrated that at least three different nanobodies can bind simultaneously to the RBD.
source: These data confirmed the separation of our major epitope bins, and furthermore demonstrated that we can bind at least three different nanobodies simultaneously to the RBD, contrasting with the much larger conventional immunoglobulins, which may be too large to simultaneously bind either monomer or trimer S protein (Corti et al., 2021; Stewart et al., 1997; Xu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on mass photometry experiments, supported by citations.

claim: 36% of the monomeric nanobody repertoire neutralized with IC50s ≤ 100 nM.
source: Overall, 36% of our monomeric nanobody repertoire neutralized with IC50s ≤ 100 nM, while 23% showed neutralization with IC50s < 50 nM and 17 potent neutralizers at 20 nM or lower (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on pseudovirus neutralization assays, supported by reference to Figure 4A.

claim: 23% of the monomeric nanobody repertoire showed neutralization with IC50s < 50 nM.
source: Overall, 36% of our monomeric nanobody repertoire neutralized with IC50s ≤ 100 nM, while 23% showed neutralization with IC50s < 50 nM and 17 potent neutralizers at 20 nM or lower (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on pseudovirus neutralization assays, supported by reference to Figure 4A.

claim: 17 potent neutralizers had IC50s at 20 nM or lower.
source: Overall, 36% of our monomeric nanobody repertoire neutralized with IC50s ≤ 100 nM, while 23% showed neutralization with IC50s < 50 nM and 17 potent neutralizers at 20 nM or lower (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on pseudovirus neutralization assays, supported by reference to Figure 4A.

claim: The most potent neutralizing nanobodies mapped to the RBD.
source: Our most potent neutralizing nanobodies mapped to the RBD; neutralizing activity mapped to each of the major epitope bins of the RBD and were of similar efficacy to the most potent of the comparison nanobodies; importantly, nanobodies binding outside of the RBD also possess neutralizing activity (for example S1-64 and S1-65).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on pseudovirus neutralization assays and epitope mapping.

source: The efficacy of the S1-23 nanobody was strongly enhanced when provided to cells as a trimer, potently inhibiting viral replication (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on ALI culture experiments, supported by reference to Figure 5C.

claim: Nanobodies inhibited at lower doses than recombinant ACE2.
source: Nanobodies inhibited at lower doses than recombinant ACE2, reflective of our measured low KD of nanobody interactions with spike (<1 nM) compared to a reported KD of 14.7 nM or greater for ACE2 with spike (Huang and Chai, 2020; Shang et al., 2020; Chan et al., 2020; Rogers et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020b; Cao et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on ALI culture experiments, supported by citations.

source: We thus identified 32 unique rVSV-SARs-CoV-2/GFP mutants that exhibited resistance to one or more of 22 representative neutralizing nanobodies against diverse spike epitopes (Table 7).

claim: Some of the mutations that arose in the selection experiments were likely passenger mutations.
source: While some of the mutations that arose in the selection experiments were likely passenger mutations (Table 7), a number of mutations clustered on the spike surface close to each other on RBD (Figure 6—figure supplement 1; Weisblum et al., 2020; Muecksch et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021b).

evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on escape variant selection experiments.

evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on escape variant selection experiments, supported by reference to Table 7.

claim: When nanobodies were combined in cocktails containing two nanobodies, in eight out of nine cases, no infectious rVSV/SARS-CoV-2/GFP was recovered after two passages.
source: In contrast, when nanobodies were combined in cocktails containing two nanobodies, at the same total concentration as was used for the individual nanobodies, in eight out of nine cases, no infectious rVSV/SARS-CoV-2/GFP was recovered after two passages (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on escape variant selection experiments, supported by reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: In the ninth case in which S1-48 and RBD-15 were combined and virus was still recovered, sequence analysis revealed that this virus contained two amino acid substitutions, F490V and Y508H, in the RBD.

evidence: This is a conclusion based on the study's findings from escape variant selection experiments.

claim: The authors used the Integrative Modeling Platform (IMP) to generate structures using multiple atomic resolution structures available for both spike and the invariant framework of nanobodies.
source: We used the Integrative Modeling Platform (IMP) (Webb et al., 2018) to generate structures using multiple atomic resolution structures available for both spike and the invariant framework of nanobodies as our starting point.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's methodology, supported by a citation.

claim: Spatial restraints for the integrative modeling calculations were based on escape mutant data.
source: Spatial restraints for these calculations were based on our escape mutant data (Table 7) because for each nanobody its escape mutants cluster around a highly restricted area of its binding epitope on spike (Garrett et al., 2021); additional residue-specific distance restraints were generated by cross-linking with MS readout (XL-MS) using the amine-specific bifunctional cross-linkers DSS and BS3 (Shi et al., 2015; Table 8).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's methodology, supported by citations and references to Table 7 and Table 8.

claim: The authors incorporated epitope binning and MP findings to provide excluded volume validation data.

evidence: This is a statement of the study's methodology, supported by citations and references to Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

evidence: This is a statement of the study's methodology, supported by a citation and reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The authors solved integrative structures for 21 different neutralizing nanobodies.

claim: Neutralizing nanobodies bind at sites that are complementary to sites of glycosylation.
source: As expected, neutralizing nanobodies bind at sites that are complementary to sites of glycosylation, which entropically shield larger zones than represented (Casalino et al., 2020), and are instead concentrated at the largely glycan-free RBD.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on integrative modeling, supported by a citation.

claim: ~80% of anti-RBD nanobodies are neutralizing.
source: Indeed, among our entire repertoire, epitope binning shows that neutralization activity, corresponding escape mutants, and the mapped epitopes are heavily concentrated on the RBD (Figures 3, 4 and 6); ~80% of our anti-RBD nanobodies are neutralizing, with many escape mutants mapping adjacent to the receptor-binding motif (RBM), the region of RBD that interacts directly with ACE2 and is most lightly glycosylated (Shajahan et al., 2020; Watanabe et al., 2020), whereas ~20% of our anti-S2 nanobodies and ~60% of our non-RBD anti-S1 nanobodies are neutralizing.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on neutralization assays and epitope mapping, supported by references to Figures 3, 4, and 6, and citations.

source: Indeed, among our entire repertoire, epitope binning shows that neutralization activity, corresponding escape mutants, and the mapped epitopes are heavily concentrated on the RBD (Figures 3, 4 and 6); ~80% of our anti-RBD nanobodies are neutralizing, with many escape mutants mapping adjacent to the receptor-binding motif (RBM), the region of RBD that interacts directly with ACE2 and is most lightly glycosylated (Shajahan et al., 2020; Watanabe et al., 2020), whereas ~20% of our anti-S2 nanobodies and ~60% of our non-RBD anti-S1 nanobodies are neutralizing.

source: Overlapping with the RBM are groups 3 (S1-48, S1-RBD-40, S1-23, S1-37, S1-36) and 4 (S1-RBD-29, S1-RBD-21, S1-62); group 3 partially overlaps with previously defined site Ia/class I and group 4 partially overlaps with site Ib/class 2; however, S1-48 uniquely extends beyond the site Ia/class 1 sitting in the saddle of the RBM.

source: Overlapping with the RBM are groups 3 (S1-48, S1-RBD-40, S1-23, S1-37, S1-36) and 4 (S1-RBD-29, S1-RBD-21, S1-62); group 3 partially overlaps with previously defined site Ia/class I and group 4 partially overlaps with site Ib/class 2; however, S1-48 uniquely extends beyond the site Ia/class 1 sitting in the saddle of the RBM.

source: Overlapping with the RBM are groups 3 (S1-48, S1-RBD-40, S1-23, S1-37, S1-36) and 4 (S1-RBD-29, S1-RBD-21, S1-62); group 3 partially overlaps with previously defined site Ia/class I and group 4 partially overlaps with site Ib/class 2; however, S1-48 uniquely extends beyond the site Ia/class 1 sitting in the saddle of the RBM.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on integrative modeling.

evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on integrative modeling, supported by citations.

claim: Group 6 is represented by a single nanobody (S1-RBD-35) and binds the RBM at a site partially overlapping with site Ib/class 2.
source: However, a number of our nanobodies map to epitopes that appear distinct from those previously described: group 6 is represented by a single nanobody (S1-RBD-35) and also binds the RBM at a site partially overlapping with site Ib/class 2 (Corti et al., 2021; Tortorici et al., 2020; Dejnirattisai et al., 2021), but is distinguished by its binding to the tip of the RBM at the left of this representation (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on integrative modeling, supported by citations and reference to Figure 6.

source: S1-46 represents group 7 and defines a unique binding site, adjacent to site IIc/class 4, but higher on the RBD and closer to the RBM.

evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on integrative modeling, supported by citations.

claim: 7 out of 10 nanobody groups do not overlap with the mutations that distinguish alpha, beta, gamma, and delta SARS-CoV-2 VOCs.
source: Of the 10 groups into which our nanobodies were classified, 7 (groups 1, 2, 5, and 7 targeting RBD; group 8 targeting the S1-NTD; groups 9 and 10 targeting S2) do not overlap with the mutations that distinguish alpha, beta, gamma, and delta SARS-CoV-2 VOCs (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on integrative modeling and comparison with VOC mutations, supported by reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The group 1 nanobody S1-1 effectively neutralized delta virus.
source: As predicted, the group 1 nanobody S1-1 effectively neutralized delta, whereas the group 6 nanobody S1-RBD-35 did not (Figure 6—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on plaque reduction neutralization assays, supported by reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The group 6 nanobody S1-RBD-35 did not effectively neutralize delta virus.
source: As predicted, the group 1 nanobody S1-1 effectively neutralized delta, whereas the group 6 nanobody S1-RBD-35 did not (Figure 6—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on plaque reduction neutralization assays, supported by reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 3B.

claim: A subset of the 21 modeled nanobodies bind sites that interfere with ACE2 binding, preventing the virus from initial binding to its host cell.
source: A subset of the 21 modeled nanobodies bind sites that interfere with ACE2 binding, preventing the virus from initial binding to its host cell (Wrapp et al., 2020b; Walls et al., 2020; Starr et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's interpretation of the integrative modeling results, supported by citations.

claim: The RBD is tethered to spike through a hinge, allowing it to fluctuate between either a 'down' conformation or an 'up' conformation.
source: The RBD is tethered to spike through a hinge, allowing it to fluctuate between either a 'down' conformation, hiding the vulnerable RBM from the host immune system, or an 'up' conformation, exposing the RBM for potential ACE2 binding and so spike activation/disassembly (Corti et al., 2021; Cai et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about the RBD, supported by citations.

claim: Group 1 nanobodies should only bind to the RBD when it is in the 'up' conformation.
source: Group 1, with overlapping and adjacent epitopes to the RBM, should only bind to the RBD when it is in the 'up' conformation (Figure 6).
evidence: This is an inference based on the integrative modeling results, supported by reference to Figure 6.

claim: Groups 3, 4, and 6 nanobodies appear agnostic to RBD conformation and may bind to both 'up' and 'down' positions of the RBD.
source: In contrast, groups 3, 4, and 6 also have overlapping and adjacent epitopes to the RBM, but appear agnostic to RBD conformation and may bind to both 'up' and 'down' positions of the RBD.
evidence: This is an inference based on the integrative modeling results.

claim: For nanobodies whose epitopes actually overlap significantly with the RBM (e.g., S1-48, S1-62, S1-RBD-15, or S1-RBD-35), neutralization may occur by directly competing with ACE2 and preventing its binding.
source: For nanobodies whose epitopes actually overlap significantly with the RBM (e.g., S1-48, S1-62, S1-RBD-15, or S1-RBD-35) (Figure 6), neutralization may occur by directly competing with ACE2 and preventing its binding.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism of neutralization based on the integrative modeling results, supported by reference to Figure 6.

claim: For nanobodies within these groups with epitopes more adjacent to the RBM (e.g., S1-36, S1-1, or S1-RBD-9), neutralization may occur through sterically occluding ACE2 binding.
source: For nanobodies within these groups with epitopes more adjacent to the RBM (e.g., S1-36, S1-1, or S1-RBD-9), neutralization may occur through sterically occluding ACE2 binding.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism of neutralization based on the integrative modeling results.

claim: Several nanobodies sharing similar epitope bins as S1-RBD-9 (group 1), such as S1-RBD-34, S1-RBD-19, S1-RBD-25, S1-RBD-32, and S1-RBD-36, do not neutralize spike.
source: However, interestingly, several nanobodies sharing similar epitope bins as S1-RBD-9 (group 1), such as S1-RBD-34, S1-RBD-19, S1-RBD-25, S1-RBD-32, and S1-RBD-36, do not neutralize spike (Table 1), suggesting that neutralization may occur via an additional mechanism.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on neutralization assays, supported by reference to Table 1.

claim: The binding of nanobodies in groups 1, 3, 4, and 6 may mimic ACE2 binding, thus trapping the RBD in its 'up' position to either catalyze the spike trimer rearrangements that prematurely convert spike into a post-fusion state, suppressing viral fusion, or destabilizing the trimer to cause its premature disassembly.
source: Additionally, the binding of nanobodies in groups 1, 3, 4, and 6 may mimic ACE2 binding, thus trapping the RBD in its 'up' position to either catalyze the spike trimer rearrangements that prematurely convert spike into a post-fusion state, suppressing viral fusion, or destabilizing the trimer to cause its premature disassembly (Huo et al., 2020b; Walls et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2020a; Turoňová et al., 2020; Benton et al., 2020; Cai et al., 2020; Koenig et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism of neutralization based on the integrative modeling results, supported by citations.

claim: Nanobodies in groups 2, 5, and 7 bind sites distal to the RBM, and therefore are unlikely to neutralize spike through direct ACE2 competition.
source: Nanobodies in groups 2, 5, and 7 bind sites distal to the RBM, and therefore are unlikely to neutralize spike through direct ACE2 competition (Figure 6).
evidence: This is an inference based on the integrative modeling results, supported by reference to Figure 6.

claim: Group 5 (S1-RBD-16, S1-RBD-23) binds to the exposed face of the RBD, and its binding is likely to be agnostic to RBD conformation.

source: Group 5 (S1-RBD-16, S1-RBD-23) binds to the exposed face of the RBD, and its binding is likely to be agnostic to RBD conformation, and group 2 (S1-6) binds at a position adjacent to group 1, which is enough of a shift that it also may bind both 'up' and 'down' RBD conformations.

evidence: This is a statement supported by citations.

claim: The S2 domain is not where the great majority of mutants in the current VOCs map, making it a particularly exciting target for potentially universal and VOC-resistant therapeutics.
source: It is also not where the great majority of mutants in the current VOCs map, making it a particularly exciting target for potentially universal and VOC-resistant therapeutics.

source: For example, the S2-10 escape mutant S982R (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) indicates binding at S982 of spike, positioned at the end of the highly conserved heptad repeat 1, within a region of the S2 that undergoes large dynamic changes as the protein adopts a post fusion conformation; this suggests that S2-10 may restrict this conformational change, thereby inhibiting viral fusion (Cai et al., 2020; Pierri, 2020; Turoňová et al., 2020; Walls et al., 2020).

source: For example, the S2-10 escape mutant S982R (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) indicates binding at S982 of spike, positioned at the end of the highly conserved heptad repeat 1, within a region of the S2 that undergoes large dynamic changes as the protein adopts a post fusion conformation; this suggests that S2-10 may restrict this conformational change, thereby inhibiting viral fusion (Cai et al., 2020; Pierri, 2020; Turoňová et al., 2020; Walls et al., 2020).

claim: The region proximal to S982 appears accessible through an ~30 Å portal, even in the prefusion form with the RBDs in the 'up' position.
source: Notably, the region proximal to S982 appears accessible through an ~30 Å portal, even in the prefusion form with the RBDs in the 'up' position.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on integrative modeling.

source: This is a size not inconsistent with the binding face of a diminutive nanobody but likely inaccessible to conventional antibodies, as has been suggested by others (Xu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference based on the integrative modeling results, supported by a citation.

claim: S2-40 uniquely sits at the interface between spike subunits.
source: S2-40 uniquely sits at the interface between spike subunits, which raises fascinating possibilities for its neutralizing activity, perhaps involving the alteration of spike's quaternary structure or dynamics.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on integrative modeling.

claim: Dimerization of S1-7 and S1-25 did not convert them into neutralizers.
source: In some cases, for example, S1-7 and S1-25 (which are non-neutralizing as monomers), dimerization did not convert them into neutralizers.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on neutralization assays.

claim: Dimerization and trimerization can engender several folds to orders of magnitude increased neutralization potency (e.g., S1-RBD-35 and S1-23, respectively).
source: In other cases, dimerization and trimerization can engender several folds to orders of magnitude increased neutralization potency (e.g., S1-RBD-35 and S1-23, respectively) (Figure 4, Table 4).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on neutralization assays, supported by reference to Figure 4 and Table 4.

claim: S2-7 is essentially non-neutralizing as a monomer but becomes strongly neutralizing upon dimerization.
source: We even have a curious case where a nanobody such as S2-7 that is essentially non-neutralizing as a monomer becomes strongly neutralizing upon dimerization (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on neutralization assays, supported by reference to Figure 4.

claim: Aggregation is a possible contributory mechanism for the neutralization enhancement observed upon dimerization of S2-7.
source: In this latter case, aggregation is a possible contributory mechanism, both between virions – which would lower effective virion concentration – or within a virion, with adjacent spike trimers being cross-linked to each other, inhibiting their function.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the study's findings.

claim: There is likely a limit to how much improvement can be induced by oligomerization.
source: Although a tremendous range in neutralization improvements by oligomerization is observed both by us and others, there is likely a limit to how much improvement can be induced by oligomerization as, for example, the trimers of S1-23 and S1-RBD-35 do not show a similar fold improvement as to what was observed for the monomer to dimer transition (Figure 4D, Table 4; Schoof et al., 2020; Xiang et al., 2020; Koenig et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the study's findings, supported by citations and references to Figure 4D and Table 4.

claim: Tixagevimab and cilgavimab, two human monoclonal antibodies that target non-overlapping regions of the RBD, function synergistically and show promise as prophylactic and therapeutic agents against COVID-19.
source: For example, tixagevimab and cilgavimab, two human monoclonal antibodies that target non-overlapping regions of the RBD, function synergistically and show promise as prophylactic and therapeutic agents against COVID-19 (Dong et al., 2020; Zost et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations.

claim: A major advantage of a large repertoire of nanobodies that bind to different epitopes on spike is their strong potential for cooperative activity among nanobody pairs (or higher-order combinations), leading to synergistic viral-neutralizing effects.
source: A major advantage of a large repertoire of nanobodies that bind to different epitopes on spike is their strong potential for cooperative activity among nanobody pairs (or higher-order combinations), leading to synergistic viral-neutralizing effects.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's rationale for testing nanobody combinations.

claim: The small size of nanobodies provides a great advantage over much larger immunoglobulins in the context of cooperative activity because the binding of a nanobody has a lower chance of sterically occluding the binding of a second nanobody to a distinct epitope and because they are monovalent.
source: The small size of nanobodies also provides a great advantage over much larger immunoglobulins in this context as the binding of a nanobody has a lower chance of sterically occluding the binding of a second nanobody to a distinct epitope and because they are monovalent.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's rationale for testing nanobody combinations.

claim: Nanobodies binding to the RBD may stabilize the otherwise 'up'-'down' fluctuating RBD in its 'up,' ACE2-engaging, position.
source: Moreover, as discussed above, nanobodies binding to the RBD may stabilize the otherwise 'up'-'down' fluctuating RBD in its 'up,' ACE2-engaging, position (Figure 6; Xiang et al., 2020; Schoof et al., 2020; Bracken et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's interpretation, supported by citations and reference to Figure 6.

claim: Stabilizing the RBD in the 'up' position will increase the effective on rate for spike trimer to that measured for monomer, making it easier for complementary nanobodies to bind and inhibit.
source: This can have three effects, all of which can potentially promote nanobody synergy: first, it will increase the effective on rate for spike trimer to that measured for monomer, and therefore, make it easier for complementary nanobodies to bind and inhibit; second, by stabilizing this 'up' for any one of the three RBDs in each spike trimer, it destabilizes the 'down' position for the remaining two RBDs, again making nanobody binding from the second class more likely; and third, the 'up' position exposes additional nanobody epitopes that would otherwise be buried (Figure 6; Xiang et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism for nanobody synergy based on the study's interpretation, supported by citations and reference to Figure 6.

claim: Stabilizing the 'up' position for any one of the three RBDs in each spike trimer destabilizes the 'down' position for the remaining two RBDs, making nanobody binding from the second class more likely.
source: This can have three effects, all of which can potentially promote nanobody synergy: first, it will increase the effective on rate for spike trimer to that measured for monomer, and therefore, make it easier for complementary nanobodies to bind and inhibit; second, by stabilizing this 'up' for any one of the three RBDs in each spike trimer, it destabilizes the 'down' position for the remaining two RBDs, again making nanobody binding from the second class more likely; and third, the 'up' position exposes additional nanobody epitopes that would otherwise be buried (Figure 6; Xiang et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism for nanobody synergy based on the study's interpretation, supported by citations and reference to Figure 6.

claim: The 'up' position exposes additional nanobody epitopes that would otherwise be buried.
source: This can have three effects, all of which can potentially promote nanobody synergy: first, it will increase the effective on rate for spike trimer to that measured for monomer, and therefore, make it easier for complementary nanobodies to bind and inhibit; second, by stabilizing this 'up' for any one of the three RBDs in each spike trimer, it destabilizes the 'down' position for the remaining two RBDs, again making nanobody binding from the second class more likely; and third, the 'up' position exposes additional nanobody epitopes that would otherwise be buried (Figure 6; Xiang et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism for nanobody synergy based on the study's interpretation, supported by citations and reference to Figure 6.

source: Combinations of S1-27 and S1-23 showed simple additive effects (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on synergy assays, supported by reference to Figure 7A.

claim: The additive effect of S1-27 and S1-23 is as expected for two nanobodies accessing the same site on S1-RBD.
source: These nanobodies belong to the same epitope bin (Figure 3A); their additive effect is as expected for two nanobodies accessing the same site on S1-RBD, but, for example, in equal concentrations, effectively doubling the concentration of a single nanobody.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings, supported by reference to Figure 3A.

claim: Powerfully synergistic effects were observed between numerous nanobody pairs that bind to different epitopes.
source: The potential for synergy resides instead in nanobodies that bind to different epitopes and can bind to spike monomers simultaneously. We therefore tested combinations that bind to different epitopes, first focusing on the RBD. Indeed, powerfully synergistic effects were observed between numerous nanobody pairs.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on synergy assays.

claim: The combination of S1-23 and S1-1 dramatically increased the potency of both nanobodies by ~32- and ~ 21-fold, respectively.
source: For example, the combination of S1-23 and S1-1, which bind to opposite sides of the RBD, dramatically increased the potency of both nanobodies by ~32- and ~ 21-fold, respectively (Figure 7B, Table 9).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on synergy assays, supported by reference to Figure 7B and Table 9.

claim: S1-1 is expected to bind to RBD in its 'up' position, while S1-23 can bind to both 'up' and 'down' RBDs.
source: S1-1 is expected to bind to RBD in its 'up' position, while S1-23 can bind to both 'up' and 'down' RBDs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the integrative modeling results.

source: We interpret this reciprocal synergy observed as S1-23 promoting the 'up' position and S1-1 stabilizing the 'up' position.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings based on synergy assays and integrative modeling.

source: S1-RBD-15, which binds to a similar epitope as S1-1, shows corresponding synergy with S1-23, suggesting that synergy may be predictable based on epitope mapping (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on synergy assays, supported by reference to Figure 7C.

claim: S1-RBD-15 had a greater influence on S1-23, promoting its potency by ~300-fold.
source: In this case, however, S1-RBD-15 had a greater influence on S1-23, promoting its potency by ~300-fold.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on synergy assays.

source: However, it should not be taken for granted that simply binding to distinct epitopes on RBD simultaneously will always be sufficient to generate a strongly synergistic response. For example, S1-46 failed to show synergy with either S1-23 or S1-RBD-15 (Figure 7E and F).

source: Indeed, synergy modeling indicates that S1-46 actually mildly antagonizes both S1-23 and S1-RBD-15 (Table 9).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on synergy modeling, supported by reference to Table 9.

source: S1-46 binds an epitope on RBD only in the 'up' position (Figure 6), but in this case binding hinders the movement of adjacent RBDs, and therefore reduces the activity of nanobodies depending on the dynamics of adjacent RBDs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings based on synergy assays and integrative modeling, supported by reference to Figure 6.

claim: S1-49, which binds to the NTD of spike, substantially improved the neutralization potency of either S1-1 or S1-RBD-15.
source: S1-49, which binds to the NTD of spike (Figure 6), substantially improved the neutralization potency of either S1-1 or S1-RBD-15 (Figure 7G and H).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on synergy assays, supported by references to Figure 6, 7G, and 7H.

claim: The synergy observed with S1-49 with S1-1 elicited a >1000-fold increase in potency.
source: The synergy observed with S1-49 with S1-1 elicited a >1000-fold increase in potency.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on synergy assays.

source: Interestingly, among all the nanobody pairs that we tested, the synergy was greatest with the S2-10-dimer, which showed >4000-fold increase in potency when combined with either S1-23 or S1-RBD-15 (Figure 7I and J).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on synergy assays, supported by reference to Figure 7I and J.

source: S2-10 recognizes a site occluded by the S1-RBD when it is in its 'down'' position, but is revealed and becomes accessible when in its 'up' position.

source: Thus, we interpret the mechanism of synergy as one of cooperativity where these RBD-binders promote the 'up' state and provide increased access for S2-10.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings based on synergy assays and integrative modeling.

source: The strong synergy observed may also reflect the distinct mechanisms by which either the RBD-binders or S2-10 operate individually.

source: Our repeated observation of strong synergistic effects between nanobodies is especially noteworthy, reflecting the unique properties of nanobodies such as their small size that are not shared by, for example, human monoclonal antibodies.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the study's findings.

evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on structural modeling.

source: In the case of S1-23 and S1-RBD-15 epitopes, structural alignment of IgGs with nanobody paratopes suggested a strong inter-IgG steric clash in addition to a clash with other RBDs in the down position.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on structural modeling.

claim: Various modifications, such as albumin-binding domains or a synthetic Fc, are available to tune half-life and other behaviors of nanobodies upon either intravenous or intranasal delivery.
source: While native nanobodies' small size and lack of an Fc domain affect their pharmacokinetic behavior in comparison to standard IgGs when used therapeutically, numerous studies have demonstrated that various modifications, such as albumin-binding domains or a synthetic Fc, are available to tune half-life and other behaviors upon either intravenous or intranasal delivery (Tijink et al., 2008; Nambulli et al., 2021; Pymm et al., 2021; Shen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations.

claim: The data demonstrate the power of raising large and diverse repertoires of nanobodies against the entire ectodomain of SARS-CoV-2 spike to maximize the likelihood of generating potent reagents for prophylactics and therapeutics.
source: The data presented here demonstrate the power of raising large and diverse repertoires of nanobodies against the entire ectodomain of SARS-CoV-2 spike to maximize the likelihood of generating potent reagents for prophylactics and therapeutics.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's findings.

claim: Several neutralizing nanobodies in the current repertoire are, or are predicted to be, effective against current circulating variants.
source: Moreover, several neutralizing nanobodies in our current repertoire are, or are predicted to be, effective against current circulating variants (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).

claim: The escape experiments support the idea that the current circulating variants are not yet necessarily exploring the full potential of the virus to escape current and emerging therapeutic arsenals.
source: However, our escape experiments support the idea that the current circulating variants are not yet necessarily exploring the full potential of the virus to escape our current and emerging therapeutic arsenals, and that even if antibodies or nanobodies are resistant to the current variants, they will not necessarily be resistant to variants as they continually emerge.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the study's findings from escape variant selection experiments.

source: To counteract this eventuality, we show that judicious choice of nanobody combinations that can synergize and have orthogonal and complementary neutralization mechanisms have the potential to result in potent and broadly neutralizing reagents that are resistant to viral escape.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the study's findings from synergy and escape variant selection experiments.

claim: This unique and readily modifiable repertoire has the potential to complement vaccines, drugs and single epitope reagents, and guard against single-molecule failure in human trials even in the face of emerging variants.
source: Collectively, this unique and readily modifiable repertoire has the potential to complement vaccines, drugs and single epitope reagents, and guard against single-molecule failure in human trials even in the face of emerging variants.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the study's findings.

claim: The repertoire paves the way to develop therapeutics for hospitalized patients with acute disease, and address the unmet needs of patients in the developing world, many of which will not see a COVID-19 vaccine before 2023.
source: Most urgently, it paves the way to develop therapeutics for hospitalized patients with acute disease, and address the unmet needs of patients in the developing world, many of which will not see a COVID-19 vaccine before 2023 (Padma, 2021).
